description:
Hi! I'm Shaafi, a young coder from the UAE who loves space, technology and building apps.

About me: I build apps and games in MIT App Inventor. For my school's science exhibition, I built the technical part of an AI-powered smart sustainable school model, with solar energy, smart sensors and ideas for saving resources.

My interests: Space exploration, Mars missions, game design, robotics and sustainable technology.
summary: Mission Builder 3D is an offline browser game for young people, created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge’s Space Mission Design Game. Players take the role of a Mars mission manager: they choose a rocket, science instruments, a power source and an antenna, then work through six launch checks and guide their lander through 20 sols on Mars. The game makes mission design approachable by letting players see how choices about mass, budget, power and communications affect one another. Dust, storms, battery use and the time it takes signals to travel between Earth and Mars add challenges to the mission. By experimenting with designs and learning from the mission report, players can explore real spaceflight trade-offs in an interactive 3D setting. The game brings real Mars exploration into the experience through NASA data and imagery, while its mission challenges and scoring are created for gameplay.. It is a student project and is not endorsed by NASA.
details:
Mission Builder 3D is a browser-based game that puts players in charge of a Mars lander mission. Players choose a rocket, science instruments, a power source, and an antenna while balancing cost, mass, and energy. Six launch checks explain any problems with the design and let players improve it before liftoff.

After landing, players manage the lander for 20 Martian days, or *sols*. They choose a safe landing site, carry out hands-on science tasks, manage power during dust and storms, and send commands across the Earth–Mars distance. Commands take effect only after their simulated signal arrives. The final report counts the science that actually reaches Earth, alongside budget and green mission points.

The project aims to make the trade-offs behind a space mission visible and engaging. Players learn that collecting science depends on more than carrying instruments: the spacecraft must have enough power to operate them and enough communication capacity to return their findings. Four mission scenarios encourage players to test different strategies.

Our creative features include an automatic solar-panel cleaning brush that uses energy, a playable signal delay based on NASA/JPL distance data, and a green score that encourages players to consider reusable rockets and cleaner operation. The green score is a game feature, not an official NASA measure.

We developed the game with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Vite, and Vitest. Blender and Python were used to create the 3D assets and prepare data. It runs in a web browser without special hardware or a live data connection. Claude Code assisted with implementation; our team defined the concept, game rules and values, reviewed the work, and play-tested it.

We considered scientific accuracy, clear source attribution, accessibility, performance on different computers, and the balance between realism and enjoyable play. The game labels NASA data, calculations, and team assumptions separately so players can tell them apart.
